query: Consider the following context: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered promising candidate materials for next‐generation nuclear reactors due to their superior mechanical strength, irradiation resistance, and thermal stability at high temperatures. However, the significant positive heat of mixing between refractory alloying elements and Cu, commonly used in cooling systems, poses challenges in forming composite structures. In that context, which method can be used for large‐scale reaction and stable microstructure, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A reactive consolidation method using SPS-enabled in‐situ reaction can be employed to form a stable refractory HEA-Cu composite. In this method, rapid heating and short dwell times allow the refractory elements to react and form a uniformly distributed intermetallic or solid-solution phase without extensive elemental segregation due to the positive heat of mixing with Cu.
generation.material_initial_state: A powder blend of refractory high‐entropy alloy precursors and Cu, where the refractory elements have a strong positive mixing enthalpy with Cu.
generation.intervention: Application of spark plasma sintering (SPS) with an in-situ reaction protocol (reactive SPS) to consolidate the blend.
generation.conditions: High-temperature, high-pressure, and rapid heating conditions are applied to trigger a self-sustaining reaction during sintering while limiting excessive diffusion and phase separation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a finely distributed interfacial reaction layer (either an intermetallic or a solid-solution phase) between the refractory phase and the Cu matrix mediates the microstructural evolution.
generation.mechanism: The rapid heating and short dwell time inherent to SPS allow the reaction to proceed to completion before long-range diffusion leads to phase segregation. This reaction-driven microstructural control helps overcome the positive heat of mixing challenge, stabilizing the composite structure on a large scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: A composite with a stable, uniformly reacted microstructure that retains high temperature mechanical strength and irradiation resistance while maintaining effective thermal conductivity provided by the Cu phase.
generation.baseline: Conventional sintering or melting methods typically lead to phase inhomogeneity because the positive heat of mixing between refractory elements and Cu promotes segregation and unstable interfaces.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness may be limited by precise control of the sintering parameters; if the heating rate or dwell time is inappropriately selected, excessive diffusion or incomplete reaction might occur, compromising microstructural stability.
generation.uncertainty: While the reactive SPS approach is promising for imparting a stable microstructure, the exact phase formation paths and interfacial chemistries between refractory elements and Cu under these conditions remain to be fully elucidated and may vary with the specific alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from identical powder blends of refractory HEA constituents and Cu: one set consolidated using reactive spark plasma sintering (with rapid heating and short dwell time) and a control set using conventional sintering. Characterize the phase composition and interfacial microstructure via SEM/EDS and XRD, and then subject both sets to high-temperature stability tests and mechanical property evaluations.
measurements: Mechanical strength at elevated temperatures (compression/tensile tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reactive SPS samples do not exhibit a more uniform and stable microstructure (i.e., if there is evidence of significant phase segregation or the formation of deleterious brittle phases) compared to the conventional sample, or if the mechanical/thermal properties are not measurably improved, then the hypothesis that reactive SPS produces a large-scale stable composite via in-situ reaction is falsified.

Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ].
